entries.narration: Before we touch a single Databricks feature, it is worth asking what the finished data is for, because every decision in this course is judged against that. A data product is a table that somebody depends on, and the people who depend on it can feel four things: how fresh it is, how correct it is, what it costs, and who is allowed to read it. Take one feed of retail orders and three readers. The numbers on screen are assumptions I chose to show the trade-offs, not measurements from a real company. The finance team closes the books once a day. It needs yesterday's totals by six in the morning, right to the cent, with every order counted exactly once, and for finance a wrong number is far worse than a late one. The store dashboard is read all day long. Numbers about fifteen minutes old are fine, as long as the counts match what the tills saw, and here a late number is worse than a slightly rough one. The analyst studies years of history at once. Tomorrow is soon enough, but there must be no duplicates and no lost versions, because history that was thrown away cannot be rebuilt. Now look at the table at the bottom. Every one of those wishes has a price. Fresher data means more runs, or a stream that never stops, and that is paid in compute. Stricter correctness means checks, a quarantine and a reconciliation, and that is paid in latency. Longer history is paid in storage, and tighter access in engineering time. So one design rarely suits all three readers equally, and the first decision is whose need sets it. The common mistake is to assume fresher is always better. If finance reads a total once a day, refreshing it every fifteen minutes costs money and buys nothing. Keep the four questions on the right, because every course after this one comes back to them. Next, the three names you will meet everywhere: Spark, Delta and Databricks.

Three names come up in almost every Databricks conversation, and they are easy to blur together. The cure is to give each one exactly one job. Apache Spark is an engine. It takes a query, splits it into tasks, and runs those tasks across many machines at once, for SQL, for DataFrames and for streams. What Spark does not do is store anything. It reads files and writes files, and when the job ends, nothing of it remains except what it wrote. Spark has its own course in this series, so here we take only what we need. Delta Lake is a table format. It turns a folder of Parquet files into a table by writing a transaction log beside them. Because every change is a commit in that log, a write lands whole or not at all, and the table gains versions, history, MERGE and schema enforcement. It is important to see that Delta is files and a log. There is no Delta server running anywhere. Both Spark and Delta are open source, and this course runs both of them on an ordinary machine. Databricks is a platform, and a commercial service. It runs Spark and Delta for you, on compute it creates and manages, and it adds the things a team needs around them: Unity Catalog, which names every table and decides who may read it; ingestion tools, declarative pipelines and scheduled jobs; and the workspace, deployment and monitoring. Some of those, like Unity Catalog, also have open-source versions now, but in this course they are taught as the platform documents them. The table underneath is the test of whether the layers are clear. Running a query on fifty machines is Spark's job. Which files make up a table right now, or what it looked like yesterday, is answered by Delta's log. Who may read the gold table is Unity Catalog's question, and what starts the job at five in the morning is the job scheduler's. The last column says which course builds each answer. Next, the idea that ties these layers together: the lakehouse.

For a long time, a company that wanted both data engineering and business reporting ran two systems. On the left is that design. Raw files land in a data lake, which is cheap cloud storage that holds anything but offers no transactions, so two writers can leave a half-finished mess. Every night a copy job reshapes the files and loads them into a warehouse, a database with its own closed storage format, because that is where SQL and dashboards run well. It works, but notice what it costs. There are two copies of the data, kept in step by a job that can fail. Access rules are defined twice, once on the files and once in the warehouse. And the dashboards only see data after the nightly copy has finished. On the right is the lakehouse. There is one copy, in open files in your own cloud storage. Those files are Parquet with a Delta log beside them, so they get transactions directly, without a second database. One catalog sits over them and holds the names, the grants and the lineage. And every kind of engine reads that same copy: SQL and BI tools, Spark jobs and streams. The table at the bottom sums up what changes: one copy instead of two, open files throughout, transactions on the files themselves, access rules defined once, and SQL that sees a write as soon as it commits rather than the next morning. It is worth being honest about what a lakehouse does not remove, which is the list on the right. Raw files still have to be cleaned into good tables; that is most of this course. The size and arrangement of files still decide how fast queries run. And one copy only helps if nobody quietly makes a second one. The lakehouse is an architecture, not a product, and Databricks is one way of running it. Next, the most common way of organising the tables inside it: bronze, silver and gold.

Inside a lakehouse, tables are often organised in layers called bronze, silver and gold. Bronze keeps what arrived, as close to the source as possible. Silver makes it trustworthy. Gold answers one business question. Rather than describe them, let's push eight real orders through all three. These tables come from a local run of Spark and Delta, the same versions this whole course uses. Bronze, on the left, holds eight rows, and every column is text, because bronze does not judge. Look closely and you will find two problems. Order four appears twice, a resend with identical values. And order seven has the amount n slash a, which is not a number at all. To build silver, the job casts the store and the amount to real types, keeps one copy of each identical row, and refuses any row whose amount cannot be read as a decimal. Silver has six rows. Gold keeps only the completed orders and adds them up per store. Store seven has two orders and sixty-five. Store nine has one, for fifteen, because its other order was cancelled. Store twelve has one, eighty. The total is one hundred and sixty. Now the step that people skip: account for every row. Eight rows in bronze equals six in silver, plus one resend that was merged, plus one row that was rejected. If those numbers did not add up, we could not trust anything downstream. Here is the caution that matters most, and it is the table on the right. Calling a table silver guarantees nothing. That a write lands whole comes from the Delta log. That only finance can read gold comes from Unity Catalog grants. That order seven is set aside and counted, rather than silently lost, comes from the job's quality rules. And that gold is fresh by six comes from the schedule and its alerts. Each of those is a course of its own. And not every flow needs three layers; use the pattern where it helps. Next, the project we will build.

Databricks is a big platform, and a tour of its features would be long and forgettable. So instead we will build one project, a retail lakehouse, from an empty folder, and learn each part of the platform at the moment the project needs it. This is the finished project. On the left are its sources, landed in cloud storage. Order files arrive from the stores, one file per arrival, and sometimes the same order is sent twice. A change feed carries customer updates: new customers, changed addresses, and deletions. And a small reference table maps stores to cities: seven is Leeds, nine is York, twelve is Hull. In the middle are the Delta tables, all named and governed in one catalog. Bronze keeps what arrived. Silver is typed, deduplicated and enriched, with bad rows quarantined rather than lost. Customers keep their full history. And gold holds sales per city and per day. Under each piece is the course where we build it. On the right are the consumers from the first section, reading gold through grants. The table is gold for the sample day after the whole course's cleaning rules have run: Leeds seventy-five from three orders, York fifteen, Hull eighty. The middle band is how the project runs on the platform: as a declarative pipeline, as a scheduled job, measured for speed and cost, and deployed with a bundle and tests. I should be clear about one thing now, because it applies to the whole course. Everything that open-source Spark and Delta can do, we actually run, and every number on screen is what that run printed. What only the platform can do, like grants, Auto Loader, pipelines and jobs, is shown as real configuration from the project, checked against the documentation, and labelled as documented rather than run. Around the project are the courses about the platform itself, about table reliability, change, and finally defending the whole design. Next, how the platform actually runs your code.

When you log in to Databricks and run a query, three different places are involved, and they belong to two different accounts. Knowing which is which answers most questions about security and cost before they are asked. This frame follows the Databricks documentation for AWS; none of it is something we run in this course. On the left is the control plane. It lives in Databricks' own cloud account, and it is everything Databricks operates for you: the web application and the API, the workspace configuration, your job definitions and schedules, the cluster manager that starts compute, and Unity Catalog, which holds the names of your tables and who may read them. In the middle is the compute plane, where data is actually processed, and it comes in two kinds. Classic compute is virtual machines in your own cloud account, inside your own network. You pay the cloud provider for the machines, and Databricks for its units of work on top. Serverless compute runs in Databricks' account instead, in the same region as your workspace. Databricks starts and sizes it, there are no machines for you to manage, and there is one bill. On the right is your cloud storage: buckets in your own account. Every table's files live here, the Parquet data and the Delta log, along with the landing zone for raw files, and a workspace storage bucket for the platform's own system data, logs and results. Read the table at the bottom with our project in mind. The nightly job's definition and schedule are in the control plane. The machines that run it are in whichever compute plane you choose. Bronze, silver and gold are files in your bucket. And the rule that says who may read gold lives in Unity Catalog. So, as the list says, your data at rest stays in storage you own, the code runs wherever the compute is, and storage and compute are separate bills and separate decisions. Next, the boundaries above a single workspace.

A single query runs inside a workspace, but the workspace is not the top of the tree, and it is not the boundary most people assume it is. This frame is the documented structure, drawn for our retail company. The names on it are ours, not a real account. At the top is the account. It holds billing, it holds every workspace, and it holds identities. Users like Ana, groups like finance and store managers, and service principals, which are identities for software, like the one our scheduled job will run as. Identities are managed once, at the account, and then assigned to the workspaces they need. Inside the account is the metastore, and there is one per region. It is Unity Catalog's top-level container, and it holds every catalog of data in that region. Both of our workspaces sit in the same region, so they attach to the same metastore. Retail dev is where we build, and retail prod runs the scheduled job and serves the dashboards. Now the important part. Because both workspaces share one metastore, a table is not inside a workspace. The data lives in catalogs, and a catalog can be bound to particular workspaces. Here the development catalog is visible only in dev, and the production catalog is bound to prod, and readable but not writable from dev. The table on the right lists the boundaries and what each one separates. The account separates billing, users and regions. The metastore holds every catalog in a region. A workspace separates notebooks, jobs and compute. A catalog binding decides which workspace sees which data. And underneath it all, the cloud account separates buckets and networks. Three mistakes follow from this, and they are in the list. A workspace is not a data boundary. A grant follows its identity into every attached workspace. And development is separated from production with catalogs and bindings, not by copying data. Course 4 builds all of this. Next, the compute that actually runs our code.

Databricks offers several kinds of compute, and the most useful way to tell them apart is to ask two questions: what is it made for, and what does it cost while it is doing nothing? The table at the top answers both, from the documentation. I will not quote prices or start-up times, because they change with the cloud, the region and the plan. An all-purpose cluster is for notebooks and exploring, often shared by a few people. Its machines are in your account, and it keeps billing while idle until it auto-terminates. Job compute is created for one run of a job and removed when the run ends, so there is no idle time to pay for. A classic or pro SQL warehouse serves SQL and dashboards from machines in your account, and bills until it auto-stops. A serverless SQL warehouse does the same job on Databricks' machines, and its auto-stop can be set much shorter. And serverless compute for notebooks, jobs and pipelines keeps no machines waiting for you at all. Now apply it to our project, in the table at the bottom left. This is a provisional choice, and Course 11 revisits it with measurements. Ana, building the project, explores in notebooks on a small all-purpose cluster with a short auto-termination, so an evening away does not cost a night of machines. The nightly job that builds bronze, silver and gold runs on job compute or serverless jobs, which exist only while it runs. The store dashboards query all day, so they get a SQL warehouse. And finance's single query at six in the morning uses that same warehouse, which is already there. A few words you will meet are on the right. A DBU is the unit Databricks bills compute in. Auto-termination stops an idle cluster after a number of minutes. Access mode decides whether a cluster is shared, called standard, or dedicated to one user, and Unity Catalog needs one of the modes that support it. Next, what actually runs on that compute: the Databricks Runtime.

Every cluster and every job on Databricks runs a Databricks Runtime, and it is worth knowing what is inside one, because this course does not use it. A Runtime is a release, chosen per cluster or per job. According to its release notes, each one pins a version of Apache Spark, and bundles Delta Lake with some table features that only Databricks has, along with Auto Loader, the connection to Unity Catalog, the optional Photon engine, and a version of Python and Java with a set of libraries already installed. Long-term support releases are maintained for longer than the others, and serverless compute chooses the version for you. On the right is what this course runs instead, and these values are from a real run. Python three point one three. PySpark four point zero point one, and the engine underneath it, Spark four point zero point one. Delta Lake four point zero point zero. OpenJDK twenty-one. And the master is local with two threads: one machine, two parallel tasks. Everything here is open source, and from Course 3 on, every course builds exactly this session. Why run it locally at all? Because the table at the bottom splits the platform into two halves. Spark SQL, DataFrames and streaming behave the same in both, and so do the Delta log, MERGE, history and VACUUM. Those we run, and every number on screen is what the run printed. File counts and task counts depend on how many machines did the work, so they are never compared with a cluster's. Unity Catalog and grants, Auto Loader, pipelines and jobs, Photon and predictive optimization exist only on the platform. Those are shown as the real configuration they would take, checked against the documentation, and labelled as documented rather than run. If you have a workspace, you can follow along there, and the same code will run. Just check which Spark version your Runtime pins. Next, a single query's path through the platform, and why its name has three parts.

Let's follow one query, select everything from retail dot silver dot orders, and see who answers each question along the way. Across the top is the path on the platform, as the documentation describes it. The name has three parts: the catalog, retail, the schema, silver, and the table, orders. The compute does not know where that table is. It asks Unity Catalog, which resolves the name, and checks that this user holds three privileges: use catalog on retail, use schema on silver, and select on the table. If any one is missing, the query stops here with a permission error, before a single file is touched. If all three are present, Unity Catalog returns the table's location in cloud storage, together with a short-lived credential that is scoped to that table's files and nothing else. Only then does the compute read the files from your bucket. So the catalog is not just a list of names. It is the gate between every query and the data. Below it is the same thing tried locally, and these lines and errors are from a real run. A local session has exactly one catalog, called spark catalog. A two-part name, silver dot orders, works and finds its one row, in a folder under the local warehouse directory. The three-part name fails, with the error that spark catalog requires a single-part namespace but got retail dot silver. And a grant statement is not even valid syntax locally. There is no one to grant anything to. This is why the course writes names in two ways. Code that runs uses two parts, because that is what the local session resolves. Code that is documented uses Unity Catalog's three parts, because that is what you would write on the platform. The table beside it says where each answer comes from: which table a name means, whether a user may read it, and where its files are. On the platform, Unity Catalog answers all three. Locally, nobody checks the second one at all. Next, where your code is written, and where it runs.

The last question about the platform is a practical one: where do you write your code, and where does it run? They are not always the same place. The table at the top lists the documented options. A notebook in the workspace runs on whatever compute it is attached to, and keeps its own revision history. A Git folder in the workspace holds the same notebooks and files, but versions them with real Git, with branches, commits and pulls. With your own editor and Databricks Connect, the code is on your laptop, but each query is sent to remote compute in the workspace, through Spark Connect. With your editor and local Spark, which is what this course does, both the code and the compute are on your machine. And in Course 12, a bundle deploys the code as jobs and pipelines. Below it, on the left, is what a notebook really is, underneath. When a workspace exports a Python notebook as source, it is a plain Python file. The first line says it is a Databricks notebook. Each cell is separated by a line that reads command, followed by dashes. And a cell in another language, like markdown or SQL, is kept as comment lines that start with the word magic. This one explores the bronze orders, first in Python, then with a SQL query that counts them by status. Notice that it uses the platform's three-part names, and the display function that only a workspace provides, so this one is documented, not run. Course 3 runs a notebook in this format locally. The list beside it is the choice this course makes. Code lives in files, in Git, from the next course on. It runs locally, on open-source Spark and Delta. Notebooks are for exploring, and the job imports a real Python package rather than living inside a notebook. On a workspace, the same files would sit in a Git folder, unchanged. That completes the picture of the platform. Next, we start the project itself, from an empty folder.
